text: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: should Palmetto Springs say yes to the quarry, and what would make it worth it? Then answer two questions, weigh one Florida tradeoff in Part C, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

Case closed! You weighed the benefits and the costs, and you found strategies to make the costs smaller. That’s exactly what a good town does. Next time, we’ll think like engineers: compare a few different solutions, pick the best one, and make it even better.

A classmate says Florida should always pick what’s best for the environment, no matter what. Hmm. Think about the roads and the wetland in Palmetto Springs. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

Welcome to the town hall! Six neighbors brought comment cards. Read each one and stamp it: a benefit, a cost, or a protection strategy. Then match each strategy to the cost it lowers. Listen to everyone. That’s how a town sees the whole tradeoff.

Here’s our quarry on a balance scale. Drag each card to the benefit side or the cost side. Heavy cards count more, so watch the scale tip. When every card is on, add the protection strategies. What happens to the cost side? Does it ever reach zero?

A good town needs a whole toolbox of strategies. Drop each card into its drawer: using less, fixing damage afterward, a smarter machine, or a rule everyone follows. Round two is our quarry. After that, I’ll show you a real old quarry in the Florida Keys.

No headset today? Let's draw the deal. Here's the quarry site from above. Drag each protection sticker to the spot where it helps, and watch the cost meters drop. Every one you place gets written into the permit.

Hi, I'm June Calloway! The town council sent our quarry permit back marked pending. They'll only say yes if we show how to protect Cypress Slough and the town wells. Engineers build small models first, so let's build one. Go to the OptimaED Science Lab and make a tabletop model: the dig zone, the wetland, the wells, and at least two protections. Then tell me a benefit, a cost, and how your protection helps.
All four protections are in the permit, and the council can say yes! The costs got smaller, but not zero. That's how real choices work. Now tell me how you would vote.
Capture saved! Great model, field assistant. You earned the Golden Gavel badge.

Let’s start small. Pick something you might do in the morning, like a shower or a car ride. Then sort each card. Is it something you gained, or something you used up? Sort all three. Then write about something you really did today.

Hi! I’m June Calloway, and I’m a geologist. That means I study rocks and the land. I work in Palmetto Springs, a little Florida town. A company wants to dig a rock quarry right next to our wetland. The quarry would bring road rock and jobs. But what would we lose? The town votes on Thursday. Help me weigh it.

Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: what should the last pit become, and how can the town make it better? Then answer two questions, build your own decision matrix in Part C, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

Case closed, engineer! You compared, improved and tested, and the last pit got a great new job. That wraps up the quarter, too. Next week, a brand-new kind of problem: what happens to Florida’s land when a big storm hits?

A classmate says that if we just pick the smartest scientist’s first idea, we’ll always get the best solution. Hmm. Think about the tie, the budget and the model tests. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence, then explain how they prove your claim.

Before we build the real thing, let’s test a model. Run the first test and watch the water. If something goes wrong, pick the revision that fixes it, then test again. Real engineers do this over and over.

Time to build a decision matrix for our last pit. Tap each question box, read the evidence, and give it one, two or three stars. Then check the budget. Something surprising happens! After that, pick a design and make it better.
Engineers in Florida face lots of challenges like ours. Tap each one to see the possible solutions, and the revision an engineer might make. Notice how many of the best ideas combine two solutions.

Engineers sort a plan into two kinds of rules. A limit is pass or fail, like a budget. A goal gets scored, like helping wildlife. Read each card from the town’s plan and drop it in the right box. Then tell me what you think about the city water ideas.

June here! Let’s jump twenty years into the future. The Palmetto Springs quarry is digging its very last pit, and the town has to decide what it becomes. A bird lake? A water reservoir? A floating solar farm? Today you’re my engineer. We’ll compare all three, pick one, and make it even better.

Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: what did the storm change, and was all of it bad? Then answer two questions, trace a chain for any Florida natural event in Part C, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.
A hurricane brings three dangers: strong wind, heavy rain and storm surge (ocean water pushed onto land).

Case closed! You followed a hurricane through a whole night, and you traced its effects on the land, the ecosystem and the people. You even found the good side. Next time, we’ll think like engineers and design ways to keep a town like ours safer before the next storm.

A classmate says all natural events are disasters, and the fewer the better. Hmm. Think about last night’s storm. Then think about my last reading at the spring. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

Good morning! The storm is gone, and the night’s evidence is on my table. Let’s follow the storm surge, one link at a time: the cause, the land, the ecosystem, then the people. Two cards came from a different danger, so leave them out. When you finish, I have one more reading to show you.

Here’s the storm clock. Press the button to move through the night, two hours at a time. Watch the wind, the rain and the tide gauge on the dock. When a call comes in, drag the danger that caused it onto the call. Then you can move to the next hour.

Palmetto Springs is made up, but these photos are real. They show Mexico Beach, Florida, before and after Hurricane Michael. Drag the slider to compare. Then tap each number and stamp it: land, ecosystem or people.

My weather radio just went off. Press Play and listen closely. Then tap the three dangers the storm is bringing. Careful: a place or a time is not a danger. After that, write three things you think this storm might change in our town.

Hi, it’s June. Tonight a hurricane is heading straight for Palmetto Springs. I’m at the town’s storm center, and I’ll stay up all night reading the gauges and answering calls. Look at the map in the case file. See the red zone by the bay? Those families have to leave by six o’clock. Stay with me tonight. In the morning, we’ll figure out what the storm changed.

Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: how should the Riveras rebuild? Then answer two questions, plan a fix for any Florida hazard in Part C, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

Case closed! You studied a real storm, built a house that passed every test, and made a plan for the whole town. That’s what engineers do: they can’t stop a hurricane, but they can lower the harm. Next time, it’s review time. Get ready for a mystery on Main Street.

A classmate says the only way to protect a town is the tallest, strongest wall you can build. Hmm. Think about the Riveras’ house, and think about Elm Street. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

The Riveras have their plan. Now the town council wants one for the whole town. Tap each problem from Storm Night on the map. Pick the fix that would help most, then decide: is it built, natural or a plan?

Engineers have three kinds of tools for a storm: things we build, natural helpers like dunes and mangroves, and plans people follow. Drag each photo onto the right shelf. Which kind do you think Florida towns use most?

Time to design the Riveras’ house. Pick a foundation, windows and a roof, but watch the budget. Then run the storm. If a test fails, don’t worry. Change one part and try again. That’s what engineers do.

This is a real street in Mexico Beach, four days after the storm. Tap each number on the photo and read what happened there. Then match the clues. Look closely: where did the storm do the most damage?

Hi, it’s June. Storm Night is over, and the Rivera family needs to rebuild their house on Bay Street. Remember those Mexico Beach photos? A few houses were still standing. The Riveras asked me a big question: how do we build a house that stands up to the next storm? Let’s find out together, then design one.

You’ve got all four clues. Before you write, crack the case at the top of this tab: why did so much change when only one tree fell? Then write your case report. Use the threads you found, your photo evidence and the words from today. Your answers save as you type.

Case closed. The oak was never just a tree. It was the center of a whole web. Next time, we’ll look at real numbers from Florida and ask a new question: how can you tell if a place is healthy, or out of balance? Bring your clues.

Here’s something people say: as long as we have plants and animals, the small stuff doesn’t matter. Bees, mushrooms, bacteria. Do you agree? Think about the threads you pulled today. Pick your side, choose two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

Look down, right next to where the oak stood. See those big fan-shaped leaves? That’s saw palmetto, one of the toughest plants in Florida. It’s small, but it has its own web. Read about it, then sort its five connections. This is your last clue.

When I first started studying forests, I only noticed who ate who. It took me a while to see the rest. Now, when I look at an old oak, I see a home, a food pantry and a recycling center, all in one tree. Open every number on the real live oak photo, and see how many neighbors one tree can hold.

This is the web around my oak. Each line is one connection. Scientists can’t knock down a real tree just to see what happens, so we pull threads on paper first. Before you pull, make a guess. Tap everything you think will change. Then pull and see how close you were. One of these pulls surprised me the first time.

No headset today? You can still rebuild the web. Drag each picture card to the spot around the oak where it belongs. Or tap a card, then tap a spot. For every card, ask: what is this living thing doing with the oak? Is it eating, moving pollen, living there, or breaking things down? Then write a paragraph about the day the oak fell.

Hi, field assistant! It's Dr. Reyes. This is my last sketch of the big oak, from June, before the storm knocked it down. See the blank tags? Each one marks a neighbor that needed the oak. Today you'll rebuild that web in VR. Go into the Tranquil Forest and find the biggest tree. That's our oak. Then add one living thing for each kind of connection: food, pollination, shelter, and nutrient cycling. When you're done, every tag will be filled again.
You saved your capture. Thank you, field assistant! Later, I'll walk through your forest and check every connection you built. You earned the Golden Acorn badge.

Every tag is filled! Look at your board. An owl, a squirrel, a bee, mushrooms, and people, all tied to one tree. That's why so much changed when the oak fell. Pull one thread, and the whole web shakes. Now tell me about it in your paragraph.

Before we solve anything, let’s meet the oak’s neighbors. Five visitors are tied to this tree, but they’re not all tied the same way. Read what each one does, then pick the thread that fits. Here’s a tip from the field: don’t assume every thread is about eating. Some of my favorite connections have nothing to do with food.

Hi, it’s Dr. Lena Reyes. I want to show you some photos from a place I love: a shady hammock with one giant live oak. I visited that tree for years. Then a storm knocked it down, and when I came back, so much had changed. The owl was gone. The squirrels had moved off. Mushrooms were everywhere. Only one tree fell. So why did everything change? Look at my before and after photos, then help me find the clues.

You have all four clues. Crack the case at the top of this tab first: did the manatees really jump by twelve hundred in one year? Then write your report. Build your own manatee graph in Part C, and use real numbers as your evidence. Your answers save as you type.

Case closed, field scientist. One count can fool you, but many years of numbers tell the truth. Next week, we zoom in on the living things themselves: the body parts that help Florida plants and animals survive. See you in the field.

Some people say invasive species are no big deal, because Florida has plenty of native animals. Hmm. Think about the python and lionfish files you opened. Pick your side, choose two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.
Every dot on this chart is one real flight. Start with just two of them, one year apart. Then show them all. This is my favorite chart in Florida, because it taught me not to panic over one bad year.

Buckle up. This is a practice survey flight. The same two hundred manatees live near this spring every day. Pick the weather, pick the wind, and fly. Then change one thing and fly again. Watch your count closely. I learned something about my own flight logs this way.

Some Florida stories are getting better, and some are in trouble. Open each case file and read the data. Stamp it, then find the line that really proves it. Careful: some lines are true but don’t prove anything.

No headset today? You can still help me count. Tap every square in Plot A and Plot B. Each living thing you tap goes on that plot's data sheet. Careful: bare dirt isn't a living thing! When both plots are counted, decide which one is in balance. Then write your paragraph.

Hi, field assistant! It's Dr. Reyes. Across the creek from the old oak, wild hogs moved in last year. Is that forest still in balance? Scientists don't guess. They count. So today you'll build two plots in the Tranquil Forest. Around one tree, build a healthy plot with at least five different kinds of living things. Around another tree, far away, build a plot taken over by wild hogs. Then my team can see the difference.

Both plots are counted! Look at your data sheets. Plot A has lots of different kinds of living things. Plot B is mostly wild hogs and torn-up dirt. Numbers like these are how scientists tell a healthy ecosystem from one that's out of balance. Now use your counts as evidence.
You saved your capture. Thank you, field assistant! Later, I'll walk through both of your plots and compare them. You earned the Balance Scale badge.

Here’s a field secret. Two scientists can stand in the same wetland and feel totally different about it. That’s why we don’t trust feelings. We trust numbers. Read each card and decide: could a scientist measure this, or is it just a feeling?

Welcome back! After the big oak, I had a new question: how do scientists check if a whole ecosystem is healthy? So I flew. Every winter, scientists count manatees from small planes. Look at these two flight logs. In just one year, the count jumped by more than twelve hundred. Did that many manatees really show up? Let’s find out.

You’ve got all four clues. Before you write, crack the case at the top of this tab: how does the mystery bird find food it can’t see? Then write your case report. Use your clues and the words from today. Your answers save as you type.

Case closed! That soggy notebook was about a bird built for feeling, not seeing. Every part of it fits its job. Next time, you’ll turn what you learned into a model, a drawing that explains how a body part does its job. Bring your clues.

A classmate says plants don’t really have structures, that they’re just leaves and stems. Hmm. Do you agree? Think about the plants in today’s lesson: the cactus, the mangrove, the flytrap. Pick your side, choose two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

Here’s my favorite Florida hider: the American alligator. When I paddle my kayak, sometimes all I see are two bumpy eyes and two little nostrils. Now it’s your turn to build a head. Put the eyes and nostrils where you think they belong, then sink it. Test more than one design. Which one can still watch and breathe?

Here’s a field trick. Some of the most important body parts are the ones you can’t see. Sort each card by asking one question: could I see this part from the outside, or is it hidden inside the body? Watch the last card closely. It’s about our mystery bird.

When I work in the marsh, I wear tall rubber boots so I can stand in the water without getting soaked. Some birds have something like that built right into their bodies. Pick a water depth and watch all three birds. Try every depth, and keep an eye on the bird with the longest legs.

Let’s start with the beak, because it’s the strangest part. Scientists often compare body parts to tools, because the shape tells you the job. Look at each beak, then find the tool with the same shape. A tip from the field: don’t look at the bird’s color. Look only at the shape.

Hi, it’s Dr. Lena Reyes. This morning I found something on a boardwalk at a Florida wildlife refuge: an old field notebook, soaked by the rain. Most of the pages are ruined. But four photos survived, all of the same tall pink bird. The last line is washed out. It says, this bird finds food it can’t even see by… and then nothing. Look at the photos, then help me find the clues to finish that sentence.

You’ve got all four clues. Crack the case at the top of this tab: which draft should go on the refuge sign? Then build your own model in Part C. Your answers save as you type.

Case closed for good! Draft C goes on the sign, and visitors will learn how the spoonbill finds its food. Next week, we’ll find out what happens inside an animal when it notices something: its senses, its brain, and what it does next.

Someone once told me that drawings aren’t real science. I laughed, because my notebook is full of them! What do you think? Pick your side, choose two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

Now it’s your turn to be the scientist. Pick an organism, tap a part on the real photo, and point its arrow. Then choose what the part does and which need it meets. When you finish, you’ll have a real model, just like the ones in my notebook.
Let’s upgrade a drawing, one step at a time. First a label, then an arrow, then a caption. Watch the meter at the top. It shows how close your drawing is to being a real model.

Every model I make follows the same chain. First the part. Then what the part does. Then which survival need it meets. Build a chain for four Florida organisms. Watch out: two cards in each set don’t belong in the chain.

No headset today? You can turn a photo into a model. Look at this osprey carrying a fish. First, drag each label onto the right spot. Then pick what that part does, and an arrow appears. Last, pick the survival need it helps with. Label, arrow, caption. That's a model!

Hi, field assistant! It's Dr. Reyes. The refuge loved our spoonbill sign. Now they want a model wall for the visitor center. Remember, a picture isn't a model until it explains something. So today you'll build three models in the Optima Centum Gallery. Each one has an animal, the thing its body part acts on, and an arrow between them. A hawk's talons grab a snake. A bee's tongue sips from a flower. An owl's ears hear a rat in the dark.

Three models, all on one photo! Your labels name the parts. Your arrows show what each part does. Your captions tie each part to a survival need. Now it explains how the osprey survives. Tell me about it in your paragraph.
You saved your capture. Thank you, field assistant! Later, I'll walk through your model wall. You earned the Golden Arrow badge.

Here’s a trick I use in my field notebook. When I draw an animal, I don’t just write names next to the parts. I draw an arrow from the part to whatever it acts on. One arrow can turn a drawing into an explanation. Try it with this alligator’s teeth.

Good news from the refuge! They read our case report about the spoonbill, and now they want a sign for the boardwalk where I found that soggy notebook. Three people sent drafts. One is a photo with labels. One is a beautiful old painting. One is a photo with arrows. Only one can go on the sign. Help me decide which one really explains how the spoonbill survives.

You have the clues. Before you write, decide: what really happened that night? Then write it up like a real field report. Name the steps, use the step words, and back up what you say with what you found.

Case closed. You figured out something it took me a while to see. Next time, we’ll put two very different animals side by side and build models of their pathways. Same four steps. Let’s see what that shows us.

One more camera. This one caught a heron right after the others, and it shows the whole moment from start to finish. Well, almost. One step happens where no camera can see. Sort what the camera caught, and you’ll have your last clue.

Here’s what I know about every animal reaction I’ve ever filmed. Something always starts it, and the animal always does something at the end. The middle is where the mystery hides. So we name every step, and nothing gets to hide from us.

These are the four cameras from last night. Open each one and follow what happened, step by step. Here’s what to watch for: what started each reaction? When you’ve seen all four, look at what you found. Does it tell you anything?

No headset today? You can make comic strips instead. Three volunteers sent me reports about a bear, a deer and a lizard. Each strip has four panels, one for each step. Read the report, then pick what goes in each panel, in order. Finish all three strips.

Hi, field assistant! It's Dr. Reyes. Last night I followed a panther with my field radio, but static ate part of every message. Can you help me rebuild them? Go to the Explore The Brain map. That's right, you'll be inside a giant brain, where every message ends up! Put a panther in the middle. Around it, set up four stations: a rat, a firefly, a deer and a mosquito. Then walk to each one and say its four steps out loud. Stimulus, sense organ, brain, response.
Three comic strips, twelve panels! Every strip went in the same order: stimulus, sense organ, brain, response. Now, in your paragraph, tell me what would happen if the brain step went missing.
Capture saved! Thank you, field assistant. My radio log makes sense again. You earned the Golden Antenna badge.

Before we look at my cameras, let’s look at you. Your body can do something very fast without you planning it. Try the snap test, and pay attention to what happens between the sound and your tap. That’s our first clue.

Hi, I’m Dr. Lena Reyes. I study animals in the wild, and last night my trail cameras caught something I can’t explain yet. Four animals, four places, all reacting within about two minutes. I’ve opened a case file, and I need a field scientist to help me solve it. Read the case, then start gathering clues.

Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: what caught the moths, and how did it find them? Then answer two questions, build two pathway models of your own, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

Case closed! A Florida bonneted bat clicked, listened for the echoes, and its brain did the rest. Same four steps as an eagle, just a different sense. Next week, we’ll look at families: how Florida plants and animals pass their traits to their young.

A classmate says one model is enough to understand every animal. Hmm. Think about the bat, the eagle, the bear and the crab. Could one model explain them all? Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

My volunteers drew models last night, and some of them are broken. A step is missing. A model that skips a step can’t explain what the animal did. Find what’s wrong, add the missing step, then press Run and watch the signal go all the way through.

Here’s what makes my models strong. Four steps in order. An arrow between each one, with the word signal on the arrow to the brain. And a caption about a survival need. Build one for the bonneted bat, and watch the meter fill up.

Every animal uses the same four steps, but not the same senses. Look at what each animal notices. Then give it the sense organ that can pick that up. An echo needs ears. A smell needs a nose. When all four are done, look across the models. What stayed the same?

No headset today? You can build two pathway lanes right here. One lane is for a manatee, and one is for a Florida scrub-jay. Read both reports. Tap a tile, then tap the step where it belongs. When both lanes are full, sort six notes. Is each one the same for both animals, or true for only one?

Hi, field assistant! It's Dr. Reyes. Remember the bat that hunted with echoes? On my dive in the Florida Keys, I watched a dolphin do the very same thing underwater! I sketched it on my dive slate, next to a hammerhead shark. But the water smudged my sketches. Can you rebuild them? Go to the Under The Ocean map. Put a model brain in the middle. Then build two lanes that end at the brain. One lane is a fish, two blue arrows and the dolphin. The other is a fish, two red arrows and the shark. Then say each lane's four steps out loud.
Both lanes are built, and every note is sorted! Did you see it? The four steps are the same for both animals. The stimulus and the sense organ are what change. Now tell me that in your paragraph.
Capture saved! Thank you, field assistant. My dive slate makes sense again. You earned the Silver Sonar Wave badge.

Bats make their own stimulus. A bat clicks, and the sound bounces off a moth and comes back as an echo. The quicker the echo comes back, the closer the moth is. Try it yourself: click, read the echo time, and find the moth.

Last night, my new camera by the pond filmed moths around the porch light. Eleven minutes later they were gone, and the camera saw nothing. But my bat detector heard plenty. Look at the printout in the case file: slow clicks, faster clicks, then a buzz. Something was hunting in the dark. Help me figure out how it found those moths.

Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: did my seeds get mixed up? Then answer two questions, write about a parent and its offspring, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

Case closed! My seeds weren’t mixed up. Same parent, different gardens. The flower color and leaves came from the parent, and the sun did the rest. Next time, a new question: how did that one beach sunflower make all those seeds in the first place?

A classmate says babies are basically clones of their parents. Clones are exact copies. Hmm. Think about my two sunflower pots, the spotted kittens, the manatee’s scars. Are babies exact copies? Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

A panther mother just had three kittens. She has a kinked tail, a scar on her nose, and she’s thin after a hard year. Which of those will her kittens get? Make your guess for each one, then press Next generation. Don’t worry if a guess is wrong. That’s how scientists learn.

This is my favorite test. Two seeds, same parent. You pick the garden for each pot: sun or shade, plenty of water or a little. Then grow them. Watch which traits change, and which ones never change at all. Make sure you try one pot in the shade.

Four Florida cases, three stamps. Inherited means from the parents. Environment means from where it lives, or something that happened to it. Both means a little of each. Read the facts, stamp it, then pick the fact that proves it.

No headset today? You can use the pass-it-down gate. My wood stork has ten traits on its chart. Send each one through the gate. Does it pass down to the chicks, is it both, or does it stay with the parent? Read each trait carefully. Where did it come from?

Hi, field assistant! It's Dr. Reyes. A wood stork came in for a check-up, and my volunteer left one column blank on its form: will the chicks have it? Let's practice first. Go to The Countryside map and set up a family reunion. Make three families: a bear, a deer and a barn owl. For each family, bring out the model twice, and shrink one to make the baby. Then, at each family, say one trait the baby inherited, and one trait the parent got from its environment.
All ten traits made it through the gate! Inherited traits pass down to the chicks. Traits from the environment, like the bent toe, stay with the parent. Now finish my form in your paragraph.
Capture saved! Thank you, field assistant. Now I know how to finish my form. You earned the Golden Paw badge.

Here’s a field trick. When you match a baby to its parents, don’t look at colors first. Look at the shape: the legs, the snout, the shell. Some babies wear spots or stripes that fade later. Their body shape gives them away.

Hi, it’s Dr. Reyes. Last spring I collected seeds from one wild beach sunflower on the dunes. I planted some in the sunny dune garden and some in the shady courtyard. Look at the two pots in the case file. They look so different! A volunteer thinks the seeds got mixed up. Did they? Help me find out.

Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: why were Pot B’s flower heads empty? Then answer two questions, follow one flower through all five steps, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

Case closed! My courtyard sunflower had plenty of flowers, but almost no bees, so almost no seeds. I’m planting more flowers back there to invite the bees in. Next week, we’ll follow Florida plants and animals through their whole lives, and through the seasons.

A classmate says flowers are just for looking pretty. Hmm. Think about my bag test. What happened to the flower heads the bees couldn’t reach? Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

Seeds can’t walk, but they sure do travel. Some fly. Some float. Some hitch a ride on your socks. Read each Florida seed card and figure out how it gets away from its parent. Look for clues like wings, hooks or berries.

Here’s my test. Same sunny garden, same water. On some flower heads, I tie a mesh bag. Air and sunlight get through, but bees can’t. Others stay open. You decide which heads get bags. Then wait three weeks and count the seeds. Bag at least one and leave one open, so it’s a fair test.

Five steps make a new plant. Your job is to put them in order. Ask yourself: what has to happen before a seed can even exist? Start there. When all five are in place, watch a new plant come all the way around.

No headset today? You can follow three fruits from flower to seed. Slide the time bar to watch each flower grow into a fruit. Then slice it open and save three seeds. Look closely. Where did those seeds come from?

Hi, field assistant! It's Dr. Reyes. I saved seeds from Pot A in an envelope, and I want to know: can you grow them into new seeds? Go to Farm Town and grow two full circles, one sunflower and one pumpkin. Start with Plant Seeds, then set stages one to four around in a ring, like a clock.
